parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has a root-mean-square (r.m.s.) potential difference (p.d.) of $4.2\text{V}$ and a frequency of $50\text{kHz}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text:
The alternating voltage is applied across a resistor of resistance $760\Omega$.

By considering the peak voltage, show that the maximum power dissipated by the resistor is $46\text{mW}$.

markscheme_points.text: power = V² / R = 5.9² / 760 = 0.046 W or 46 mW

hints: Hint 1: Think about what r.m.s. means for a sine wave. Is the peak value larger or smaller than the 4.2 V value, and by what factor?
Hint 2: Maximum power happens at the instant of maximum voltage. Recall how power relates to voltage and resistance at any instant.
parts.proper_answer: Peak voltage $V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times V_{rms} = \sqrt{2} \times 4.2 = 5.9\text{ V}$. Maximum power $P_{max} = V_0^2 / R = 5.9^2 / 760 = 0.046\text{ W} = 46\text{ mW}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link r.m.s. to peak**
For a sinusoidal voltage, the r.m.s. value is the peak divided by root 2. So you can work backwards to get the peak. $$V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times V_{rms}$$ $$V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 4.2 \approx 5.94\text{ V}$$ This is the largest voltage that ever appears across the resistor.

Step 2: **Use peak for maximum power**
At any instant, power in a resistor is $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ So the biggest $P$ uses the biggest $V$, which is $V_0$. $$P_{max} = \frac{V_0^2}{R} = \frac{5.94^2}{760}$$ $$P_{max} \approx 0.046\text{ W} = 46\text{ mW}$$ This is twice the average power, because power depends on $V^2$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
On Fig. 7.1, draw a smooth curve to show how the power $P$ dissipated in the resistor varies with time $t$ between $t = 0$ and $t = 40\mu\text{s}$. Assume that $P = 0$ when $t = 0$.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

markscheme_points.text: sketch shows peak(s) in power at 46 mW
correct shape (sinusoidal wave sitting on t-axis)
four cycles of repeating pattern shown, with P = 0 at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 μs

hints: Hint 1: Start from the voltage frequency of 50 kHz. What is one full period of the voltage in microseconds, and why does power go through two cycles for each voltage cycle?
Hint 2: Think about $P = V^2/R$. Since $V^2$ is always positive, can $P$ ever be negative, and when must $P$ be zero?
Hint 3: Combine the peak value from (a)(i) with the timing. How many power peaks fit between 0 and 40 microseconds, and what height should they reach?
parts.proper_answer: Curve from 0 to 46 mW, always $P \ge 0$, with shape $P \propto \sin^2$. Period of voltage is $20\,\mu\text{s}$, so period of power is $10\,\mu\text{s}$. Four full power cycles in $0$ to $40\,\mu\text{s}$ with zeros at 0, 10, 20, 30, $40\,\mu\text{s}$ and peaks of 46 mW midway between.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the timing**
Voltage frequency $f = 50\text{ kHz} = 50 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}$. $$T_V = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50 \times 10^3} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s} = 20\,\mu\text{s}$$ Power depends on $V^2$, so negative voltage still gives positive power. Power is zero twice per voltage cycle and maximum twice per cycle. So $$T_P = \frac{T_V}{2} = 10\,\mu\text{s}$$ In $40\,\mu\text{s}$ you get $40/10 = 4$ full cycles.

Step 2: **Fix the shape and levels**
Because $P = V^2/R$ and $V$ is sinusoidal starting at zero, $P$ starts at zero, rises to a peak, falls back to zero, and repeats. It never goes negative - it sits on the time axis like a row of humps. Each hump peaks at $P_{max} = 46\text{ mW}$ from (a)(i). Zeros are at $t = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40\,\mu\text{s}$, peaks at $t = 5, 15, 25, 35\,\mu\text{s}$.

Step 3: **Draw it smoothly**
Draw a smooth $\sin^2$ curve, all humps the same height and width, touching zero at the times above. Keep the peaks at 46 mW, not 50 mW.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Use your line in **(a)(ii)** to explain why the mean power dissipated in the resistor is $23\text{mW}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the humps you drew. If you drew a flat line halfway up at 23 mW, is the area above the line equal to the area below it within each hump?
parts.proper_answer: The power curve is symmetrical about $23\text{ mW}$, half the maximum, so the area above equals area below and the mean over a cycle is $23\text{ mW}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use symmetry to find the mean**
Your curve swings between 0 and 46 mW with a regular $\sin^2$ shape. The midline is $$\frac{0+46}{2} = 23\text{ mW}$$ For every bit of the curve above 23 mW there is an equal bit below it. So the average over time must be exactly the midline value, 23 mW. This also matches $P_{mean} = V_{rms}^2/R$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The alternating voltage in **(a)** is now applied to a piezoelectric crystal in air.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain what happens to the air surrounding the crystal.

markscheme_points.text: vibrations (of crystal) causes air to vibrate

hints: Hint 1: Recall the basic piezoelectric property. What does a crystal do when you put an alternating p.d. across it?
Hint 2: If the crystal faces are moving back and forth 50 000 times per second, what must they do to the air molecules touching them?
Hint 3: Compare the 50 kHz frequency to the human hearing range. What name do we give to sound above about 20 kHz?
parts.proper_answer: The alternating p.d. makes the piezoelectric crystal vibrate at 50 kHz. The vibrating crystal drives vibrations in the surrounding air, producing a longitudinal wave. As 50 kHz > 20 kHz, this is ultrasound.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Crystal vibrates**
A piezoelectric crystal changes shape when a p.d. is applied. An alternating p.d. makes it alternately expand and contract, so it vibrates at the applied frequency, here $50\text{ kHz}$.

Step 2: **Air is driven**
The crystal surfaces push and pull on the adjacent air. This creates alternating compressions and rarefactions - a sound wave travelling out through the air at the same 50 kHz frequency.

Step 3: **Identify as ultrasound**
Human hearing stops at about $20\text{ kHz}$. Since $50\text{ kHz}$ is higher, the wave is ultrasound, inaudible but carrying energy through the air.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
A second piezoelectric crystal is placed in the air near to the first crystal.

Explain the effect of the surrounding air in **(b)(i)** on the second crystal.

markscheme_points.text: (air makes) crystal vibrate, which causes an e.m.f. to be generated across the (second) crystal

hints: Hint 1: Think in reverse. If sound pressure can squeeze a crystal, what electrical effect does squeezing a piezoelectric crystal produce?
parts.proper_answer: The ultrasound pressure variations make the second crystal vibrate, and by the reverse piezoelectric effect an alternating e.m.f. is generated across it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reverse effect at the receiver**
The incoming air vibrations alternately compress and stretch the second crystal. A piezoelectric crystal under mechanical stress generates a p.d. across it, so an alternating e.m.f. of the same frequency appears. This is how the crystal acts as a microphone for ultrasound.
